buildUp: Start with the goal of a full day on battery. That sets an average power budget of just a few watts, so the heart has to be an efficient system-on-chip rather than separate hot components.
Memory goes in the same package as the chip so data travels millimetres rather than centimetres, and fast storage chips sit right beside it on a small logic board near the hinge.
Even an efficient chip can make 40 W under heavy load, so flattened heat pipes carry that heat to two thin fans that blow it out through vents under the hinge.
The battery is the biggest single item, so six thin cells fill almost all the remaining base under the keyboard and trackpad.
A thin base must not flex or the keyboard feels cheap and parts crack, so the body is milled from solid aluminium into a stiff unibody shell.
The lid is a thin screen on a hinge that must stay where you put it, with cables threading through that hinge to carry the picture, and a camera squeezed into the bezel above.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Spend energy only where it does useful work. Putting the processor, graphics and memory together on one efficient chip cuts the energy wasted shuttling data around, so a modest battery lasts all day and a pair of small fans can carry away the heat. The rest of the base is filled with battery, and the lid is almost all screen.

hardParts.title: Cooling in 15 millimetres
hardParts.why: Tens of watts have to leave a box only about 15 mm thick without the fans becoming loud or the underside too hot to rest on a lap. Heat pipes flattened to a millimetre or two still have to keep their inner channel open, and fans only about 1 cm thick must move enough air quietly.

hardParts.title: Packing in the battery
hardParts.why: The cells have to fill every spare cubic millimetre of the base, yet still leave room to swell slightly as they age, stay cool, and be removable for repair despite being glued in. Every cubic millimetre not used by something else is shaped into battery, so the cells are made very thin and sized to fill the base around the trackpad.

hardParts.title: A thin lid that stays put
hardParts.why: The hinge has to hold a half-kilogram screen at any angle, open with one finger, and survive tens of thousands of cycles. Meanwhile the display cables passing through it must flex every time without their tiny tracks cracking.

principles.explanation: Hours of use equal energy stored divided by average power, so all-day battery life comes less from a big battery than from keeping power tiny most of the time. A pack of about 70 Wh lasting 17 hours means the whole laptop averages only about 4 W. Run the chip flat out at around 40 W and the same battery lasts under 2 hours. So the trick is keeping power tiny for the long stretches when you're reading, typing or watching video.
principles.title: Battery life is just division

principles.explanation: Sending data down a wire can cost far more energy than computing with it, so this laptop keeps wires short by putting memory right beside the processor. Every wire is a tiny capacitor that has to be charged to send a signal, and longer wires hold more charge. Fetching a number from memory chips several centimetres away can take on the order of a hundred times more energy than doing arithmetic with it. Putting memory in the same package as the processor and sharing it between processor and graphics cuts distance and stops data being copied back and forth, which saves both time and energy.
principles.title: Moving data costs more than computing

principles.explanation: A heat pipe carries the chip's heat to the fans by boiling water at one end and condensing it at the other, moving heat far better than a solid copper bar of the same size. Turning water into vapour soaks up more than 2,000 joules per gram, far more than just warming it. Inside each sealed copper heat pipe, at low pressure, water boils at the hot chip end, the vapour rushes to the cooler end by the fans, condenses and gives up that heat, and a wick draws the liquid back. This loop is what lets the fans sit away from the chip.
principles.title: Heat pipes move heat by boiling water

principles.explanation: Splitting the backlight into thousands of zones that switch off behind dark parts of the picture lets this LCD show near-true blacks and brighter highlights while saving power. An LCD works by blocking a backlight, but it can't block it completely, so black areas glow faintly grey. This one's mini-LED backlight has about 2,500 zones, each of which can dim partway or go fully dark, so highlights can be driven much brighter where they are needed. The power saving comes in dark scenes, where many zones are off.
principles.title: Dimming the backlight behind the dark

firstPrinciples.problem: Give someone the power of a desktop computer that folds shut, weighs about 1.5 kg and runs a full working day away from a socket. More speed means more heat to get rid of in a body only 15 mm thick, more battery means more weight, and a bigger, brighter screen drains both, so every gain in one direction costs something in another.

questions.answer: Battery life is energy divided by power. Video playback uses dedicated, efficient circuits and a few watts in total, while heavy work can push the chip to around 40 W, draining the same 70 Wh about ten times faster.
questions.question: Why can the laptop play video for 15 hours or more but last only a few hours under heavy work?

questions.answer: There's no spare room, and batteries are heavy, so it would make the laptop thicker and heavier. Airlines also limit batteries in carry-on devices to about 100 Wh without special approval, so laptops tend to stay below that.
questions.question: Why not just put a much bigger battery in?

questions.answer: It never really moves. It senses how hard you press and a small magnetic motor taps the glass to make you feel a click, and with no power there's no tap.
questions.question: Why does the trackpad stop clicking when the laptop is switched off?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: Making a laptop fast used to mean adding power and cooling; the leap here is making it efficient instead. With processor, graphics and memory on one chip and power cut to almost nothing whenever there's no work, the same machine can stay silent and cool for everyday tasks, last most of a day, and still sprint hard when you need it.

name: Laptop
overview:
A laptop is a complete computer folded into two thin slabs joined by a hinge. The lid is almost entirely screen; everything else lives in the base, which is barely 15 mm thick: the computer itself, the battery that powers it, the keyboard and trackpad you use it with, and the fans and pipes that carry its heat away.

In laptops like this one, the computer is a single system-on-chip: the processor cores, graphics, neural engine and the main memory sit together in one package on a small logic board near the hinge, with the storage chips beside it. Keeping everything so close cuts the distance signals travel, which saves power and time. Heat from the chip travels along flat copper heat pipes to two small fans, which blow it out through vents under the hinge.

The rest of the base is mostly battery: six flat lithium-ion cells under the keyboard and trackpad, enough to run the machine for a full working day. The body is milled from solid blocks of aluminium into a stiff 'unibody' shell. The trackpad doesn't actually move; it fakes a click by tapping your finger with a tiny magnetic motor, and it senses how hard you press.

parts.description: Thin cover glass over the screen, bonded to the panel to cut reflections.

details.didYouKnow: A closed laptop presses the keyboard close to the screen, so the keys can leave faint marks on the coating over time; that is why some people slip a thin cloth in before shutting the lid.
details.howItWorks: Gluing the glass straight onto the panel removes the air gap that would otherwise add two extra reflective surfaces, so the picture looks crisper and sits closer to the surface. The glass also stiffens the thin lid and protects the soft panel layers from keys and grit when the laptop is closed. A thin coating on the outside cuts glare and helps fingerprints wipe away.
keyNumbers: Typically well under 1 mm thick
Covers a screen about 14 inches diagonally
Anti-reflective coatings can cut reflections to roughly 1 to 2 percent
details.madeOf: Thin chemically strengthened glass with an anti-reflective coating on the outer face. Glass stays perfectly flat and clear for years and resists scratching far better than plastic.

parts.name: Display glass

parts.description: LCD lit from behind by thousands of tiny LEDs in dimmable zones, for deep blacks and very bright highlights.

details.didYouKnow: Because each dimming zone is far bigger than a pixel, a small white cursor on a black background can show a faint glow around it, an effect known as blooming.
details.howItWorks: The liquid crystal layer works like millions of tiny shutters, twisting light so that each red, green or blue subpixel lets through just the right amount. Behind it, thousands of mini-LEDs are grouped into zones that the graphics hardware brightens or dims to follow the picture, so a dark corner can be nearly switched off while a bright highlight beside it is boosted. The refresh rate can rise for smooth scrolling and drop when the image is still to save battery.
keyNumbers: Roughly 3,000 x 2,000 pixels
Refreshes up to about 120 times a second
About 10,000 mini-LEDs in roughly 2,500 dimming zones
Peak HDR brightness up to about 1,600 nits
details.madeOf: Liquid crystal sandwiched between glass sheets carrying thin-film transistors and colour filters, over a backlight of tiny LEDs and light-spreading films. Mini-LEDs give far finer control of brightness than the few edge-mounted LEDs of an ordinary laptop screen.

parts.name: Mini-LED display panel

parts.description: 1080p camera module in the notch at the top of the screen, with a green light that's wired to it.

details.didYouKnow: Laptop webcams have tiny sensors compared with phone cameras because the lid is so thin, so a lot of the image quality now comes from the processing done by the main chip rather than from the optics.
details.howItWorks: A small stack of lenses focuses light onto an image sensor, and the main chip's image processor cleans up noise, balances colour and adjusts exposure before the video reaches your call. The camera sits in a notch because the lid around the screen is too thin to hide the module above it. On many laptops the indicator light is wired so that the camera physically cannot send pictures without the light being on.
keyNumbers: Typically 1080p, about 2 million pixels per frame
Usually up to about 30 frames per second
Module only a few millimetres thick
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic or glass lenses over a silicon image sensor on a tiny circuit board, behind a clear window in the display glass. The module has to be only a few millimetres deep to fit in the lid.

parts.name: Webcam

parts.description: Flexible cables that run round the hinge, carrying video and power to the screen.

details.didYouKnow: Some thin laptops from the mid-2010s became known for screen faults caused by display cables that were cut too short and slowly wore through from repeated opening and closing.
details.howItWorks: A high-speed video link carries the picture from the main chip to the screen's timing controller, while other wires feed power to the backlight, the webcam, the microphones and the lid sensors. Because the cables pass through the hinge, they bend every time the lid opens and closes, so they are routed in gentle loops with enough slack to flex without cracking. Shielding keeps the fast video signal from interfering with the wireless antennas nearby.
keyNumbers: Video link carries roughly tens of gigabits per second
Flexes through about 130 degrees as the lid opens
Tracks often only a fraction of a millimetre wide
details.madeOf: Flexible printed circuits: fine copper tracks laminated between thin layers of polyimide plastic. Polyimide survives heat and repeated bending far better than ordinary plastic insulation.

parts.name: Display cables

parts.description: Thin aluminium shell on the back of the screen, machined from a single sheet.

details.didYouKnow: The sensor that notices the lid closing is usually a Hall-effect sensor, which detects magnetic fields; that is why a strong magnet held near the right spot can make some laptops fall asleep.
details.howItWorks: The lid cover is the stiff back that keeps the thin display flat and stops it twisting when you open the laptop by one corner. Small magnets along its edge hold the lid shut, and a sensor in the base notices those magnets to put the laptop to sleep when you close it. It also shields the screen from knocks in a bag.
keyNumbers: Typically only a few millimetres thick at the edges
Aluminium is roughly a third as dense as steel
Lid and screen together weigh roughly 0.5 kg
details.madeOf: Anodised aluminium alloy, machined to shape and then given a bead-blasted or brushed finish. Aluminium gives a lot of stiffness for its weight and dissipates a little heat from the panel.

parts.name: Lid (display back cover)

parts.description: Hinge with a friction clutch that holds the screen at any angle yet opens with one finger.

details.didYouKnow: The folding clamshell design that almost every laptop uses today was popularised by a portable computer from 1982, which was also carried on Space Shuttle missions.
details.howItWorks: Inside the hinge, springy steel clutches grip a shaft with carefully set friction: enough to hold the screen still when you type or the train shakes, but little enough that the base does not lift when you open the lid. The friction is balanced against the weight of the screen, which is why the lid stays put at any angle. The display cables and often the wireless antennas run through or beside this hinge area.
keyNumbers: Typically tested for roughly 20,000 or more open and close cycles
Lid opens to roughly 130 degrees
Holding torque tuned to a lid weighing about 0.5 kg
details.madeOf: Hardened steel clutch parts and shafts, sometimes inside an aluminium cover. Steel holds its shape and friction over tens of thousands of cycles where softer metals would wear loose.

parts.name: Hinge

parts.description: Full-size scissor-switch keyboard with backlit keys; the top row includes a Touch ID power key.

details.didYouKnow: In the late 2010s some laptops used an even flatter butterfly key mechanism, but a speck of dust could jam it, and makers went back to the more forgiving scissor design.
details.howItWorks: Under each keycap, two small plastic arms cross like a pair of scissors so that the key goes straight down even if you press its corner. A rubber dome springs it back and pushes onto a membrane, closing a contact that the keyboard controller scans many times a second. LEDs and a light guide shine through the letters, and an ambient light sensor adjusts the backlight to the room.
keyNumbers: Key travel about 1 mm
Key spacing about 19 mm, the same as a desktop keyboard
Typically about 78 to 80 keys
details.madeOf: Plastic keycaps with laser-etched letters, plastic scissor mechanisms and silicone domes over a printed membrane on a metal backing plate. Keycaps are often made of tough ABS or PBT plastics.

parts.name: Keyboard

parts.description: Under every key, two small plastic arms cross like scissors to keep it level, and a rubber dome pushes it back up.

details.didYouKnow: The arms exist so that thin keys don't wobble. Without them, a press near the edge of a wide key would tilt it and jam, which is why the longest keys like the space bar often have extra support.
details.howItWorks: Each key rests on a pair of crossed arms hinged at the centre, so whichever corner you press, the whole cap moves straight down. Inside them, a small rubber dome resists your finger, then buckles suddenly for that crisp click, closes a contact, and pushes the key back up.
keyNumbers: Usually about 1 mm or so of key travel
One mechanism for each of roughly 78 keys
Keys rated for millions of presses
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic arms that clip to the keycap and to a thin metal plate, and silicone rubber domes.

parts.name: Scissor mechanisms & domes

parts.description: Thin light-guide sheet under the keys, lit by tiny LEDs, that sends light up through each translucent legend.

details.didYouKnow: The mask under each key blocks light everywhere except the legend, which is why keys glow in the shape of their letters and not around their edges so much.
details.howItWorks: Small LEDs shine sideways into a clear plastic sheet. Light travels along inside it by bouncing off its surfaces, and tiny printed dots scatter some of it upward beneath each key, where it passes through the translucent legend. A sensor can dim it to match the room.
keyNumbers: Stack only a fraction of a millimetre thick
Often one LED per key or per small group
Dims across many brightness steps
details.madeOf: A thin polymer light-guide film, reflective and masking layers, and tiny LEDs on a flexible circuit.

parts.name: Keyboard backlight

parts.description: Power button with a fingerprint sensor under a sapphire cap, linked to a secure chip that stores the fingerprint data.

details.didYouKnow: The sensor reads the electrical properties of the living skin layer just under the surface, which is why it can still work even if the outer skin of your finger is slightly worn.
details.howItWorks: When you rest your finger on the key, a ring around it notices the touch and wakes a capacitive sensor that reads the tiny ridges and valleys of your fingerprint. The image is turned into a mathematical description and checked by a separate secure processor, which only replies yes or no. Your actual fingerprint data never leaves that secure area and is not sent to the internet.
keyNumbers: Sensor resolves roughly 500 dots per inch
Chance of a random fingerprint matching roughly 1 in 50,000
Sapphire scores 9 on the Mohs hardness scale
details.madeOf: A sapphire crystal cap over a silicon capacitive sensor, surrounded by a metal detection ring. Sapphire is extremely hard and scratch-resistant, so the cap stays clear for the sensor to read through.

parts.name: Touch ID key

parts.description: Large glass trackpad that senses position and pressure; it doesn't move, the click is a haptic illusion.

details.didYouKnow: Touchpads appeared on a few laptops in the 1980s, but they only took over from little trackballs in the mid-1990s; today's huge glass pads are several times bigger than those early ones.
details.howItWorks: A grid of electrodes under the glass senses the electric field of your fingers, tracking several at once for scrolling, pinching and swiping. Force sensors near the corners measure how hard you press, so the computer can decide what counts as a click or a firmer second press. When a press is detected, it tells the haptic engine underneath to give a tap that feels like a button.
keyNumbers: About 15 x 10 cm of touch area
Usually tracks up to about 4 or 5 fingers at once
Reports finger position roughly 100 or more times a second
details.madeOf: A glass top surface over a capacitive sensor board, sitting on force sensors and a metal stiffening plate. Glass feels smooth, does not wear shiny and lets your finger glide evenly.

parts.name: Trackpad

parts.description: Magnetic motor under the trackpad that taps your finger to feel like a click.

details.didYouKnow: When the laptop is switched off, pressing the trackpad does nothing at all; with no power to the haptic engine, there is no click to feel.
details.howItWorks: The engine is an electromagnet next to a metal plate attached to the trackpad. A quick pulse of current tugs the whole glass sideways by a tiny amount and lets it spring back, and your fingertip reads that sudden jolt as a downward click. Because it is software-controlled, the click can feel firmer or softer and feels the same anywhere on the pad.
keyNumbers: Glass moves only a fraction of a millimetre
Each tap lasts roughly 10 milliseconds
Draws only a few watts in brief pulses
details.madeOf: Copper coils wound on a steel core, with steel or iron plates and springs, mounted in a cast metal frame. Steel and iron carry the magnetic field efficiently so a small coil gives a strong, sharp tap.

parts.name: Haptic engine

parts.description: Compact circuit board near the hinge carrying the chip, storage, port controllers and power circuits.

details.didYouKnow: Many of the smallest parts on a laptop board, such as capacitors and resistors, are less than half a millimetre long, smaller than a grain of salt.
details.howItWorks: The logic board connects everything: the main chip, the storage, the power circuits that turn battery voltage into the many lower voltages the chips need, and the controllers for the ports, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Ribbon cables from the display, keyboard, trackpad, battery and speakers all plug into it. Packing it near the hinge leaves the front of the base free for the battery.
keyNumbers: Typically around 10 or more copper layers
Thousands of individual components
Converts about 11 to 13 V from the battery down to below 1 V for the chip cores
details.madeOf: A multi-layer printed circuit board of glass-fibre and epoxy with thin copper layers inside, carrying thousands of tiny soldered components. Many layers let signals cross over each other without needing a bigger board.

parts.name: Logic board

parts.description: Processor, graphics, neural engine and unified memory in a single package; the heart of the computer.

details.didYouKnow: The ARM processor design goes back to a 1985 chip made for a British home computer; its first test chip used so little power that it once kept running from leakage through its signal lines with the power supply disconnected.
details.howItWorks: Instead of separate processor, graphics card and memory sticks, everything is packed into one package: high-performance and efficiency processor cores, a graphics processor, a neural engine for machine learning, and memory placed right alongside. The CPU and GPU share the same unified memory, so data does not have to be copied between them. The heat pipes carry its heat away to the fans.
keyNumbers: Roughly tens of billions of transistors
Typically about 16 to 36 GB of unified memory
Memory bandwidth up to about 270 GB per second
Uses up to roughly 40 W under heavy load
details.madeOf: Silicon dies made on a 3-nanometre-class process, mounted with memory chips on a small substrate. Smaller transistors switch faster and use less power, which is what lets the laptop be both quick and long-lasting.

parts.name: System-on-chip

parts.description: Flash memory chips soldered to the board that act as the laptop's drive.

details.didYouKnow: Flash memory was invented at Toshiba in the early 1980s; the name came from a colleague who said erasing a whole block at once reminded him of a camera flash.
details.howItWorks: Each flash chip stores data as electric charge trapped in billions of tiny cells, stacked in many layers. A storage controller, often built into the main chip, spreads writes evenly so no cell wears out early, checks for errors and encrypts everything as it is written. With no moving parts it is silent, shock-resistant and far faster than an old spinning hard drive.
keyNumbers: Typically about 512 GB to 4 TB
Reads up to roughly 5 to 7 GB per second
Cells stacked in roughly 200 or more layers
details.madeOf: NAND flash memory dies stacked inside small plastic packages soldered to the logic board. Soldering them directly saves space and power but means storage cannot be upgraded later.

parts.name: Storage chips

parts.description: Flat sealed copper tubes with a little liquid inside that boils at the chip and condenses at the fans, carrying heat fast.

details.didYouKnow: The heat pipe was invented at a US laboratory in the early 1960s for cooling space and nuclear equipment, long before it ended up in laptops.
details.howItWorks: Inside each sealed pipe is a little water under low pressure, so it boils at a modest temperature where it touches the hot chip. The vapour rushes to the cooler ends at the fans, condenses back into liquid and gives up its heat to thin metal fins, then a wick lining soaks the liquid back to the chip. This loop moves heat many times better than a solid copper bar of the same size.
keyNumbers: Typically only about 1 to 2 mm thick once flattened
Water inside boils at roughly 30 to 40 degrees C at low pressure
Can carry tens of watts of heat
details.madeOf: Copper tubes with a sintered or mesh wick inside, flattened to fit the thin case and sealed with a small amount of water. Copper conducts heat very well and does not react with water.

parts.name: Heat pipes

parts.description: Thin centrifugal blower that pulls air in and pushes it out through vents under the hinge.

details.didYouKnow: Many laptops of this kind can run everyday tasks such as browsing and writing for hours without the fans turning on at all.
details.howItWorks: The left fan draws cool air in through the vents in the bottom case, spins it outwards, and blows it across the fin stack at the left end of the heat pipes before it leaves through the slot under the hinge. Its speed is set by the main chip according to temperature, and under light work it often stops completely so the laptop is silent. A small motor in the centre is driven by the logic board.
keyNumbers: Spins up to roughly 5,000 to 6,000 rpm
Only about 1 cm thick
Uses roughly 1 W or less
details.madeOf: A plastic blower housing and impeller around a tiny brushless motor with a fluid bearing. Light plastic parts start and stop quickly and keep the noise and power use low.

parts.name: Cooling fan (left)

parts.description: Dozens of slightly uneven-spaced blades that spread the fan's noise across many frequencies so it's less annoying.

details.didYouKnow: Car tyre makers use the same trick: tread blocks of slightly different lengths spread the road noise out so it does not turn into a single droning note.
details.howItWorks: As the impeller turns, its curved blades fling air outwards by centrifugal force, which builds the pressure needed to push air through the tightly packed cooling fins. Each blade passing a point makes a tiny puff of pressure, and with even spacing these would add up to one clear whine. Uneven spacing smears that tone across many frequencies so it sounds like a soft rush instead.
keyNumbers: About 36 blades
At 6,000 rpm, 36 blades pass a point about 3,600 times a second
Each blade only a fraction of a millimetre thick
details.madeOf: Very thin moulded plastic, often a liquid crystal polymer that stays stiff even when thin. Thinner blades leave more room for air, so the fan can move more of it.

parts.name: Fan blades (left)

parts.description: Thin centrifugal blower that pulls air in and pushes it out through vents under the hinge.

details.didYouKnow: Two identical fans spinning at almost the same speed can make a slow pulsing hum called a beat; control software can keep their speeds slightly apart so the sound stays steady.
details.howItWorks: The right fan mirrors the left, cooling the fin stack at the other end of the heat pipes so heat leaves the chip in both directions. The two fans are controlled together but do not have to run at exactly the same speed. Air exits at the back under the hinge, so hot air blows away from your hands and lap instead of out of the sides.
keyNumbers: Spins up to roughly 5,000 to 6,000 rpm
Each fan moves only a few litres of air per second
Together with the left fan, removes roughly 40 W or more of heat
details.madeOf: A plastic housing and impeller around a small brushless motor, like its twin. Brushless motors have no rubbing contacts to wear out, so they last for years.

parts.name: Cooling fan (right)

parts.description: Dozens of slightly uneven-spaced blades that spread the fan's noise across many frequencies so it's less annoying.

details.didYouKnow: Dust building up on the blades and fins is the most common reason an old laptop gets louder and hotter, because the fan has to spin faster to move the same air.
details.howItWorks: These blades work just like the left fan's, pulling air in at the centre and throwing it outwards into the curved housing, which guides it to the exhaust. The housing's spiral shape slows the air and turns its speed into pressure. Keeping the gaps between blade tips and housing tiny stops air from leaking back round.
keyNumbers: About 36 blades
Impeller roughly 5 cm across
Blade tips move at up to roughly 15 metres per second
details.madeOf: Thin moulded plastic, often a stiff liquid crystal polymer. A rigid, balanced impeller avoids wobble, which would cause vibration and extra noise.

parts.name: Fan blades (right)

parts.description: One of six flat lithium-ion pouch cells that together store about 70 watt-hours.

details.didYouKnow: The lithium-ion battery earned three scientists the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the first commercial cells went on sale in 1991.
details.howItWorks: Inside the pouch, lithium ions shuttle from a graphite anode to a metal-oxide cathode as the laptop runs, pushing electrons round the outside circuit to power it. Charging drives the ions back again. This outer cell sits at the left front of the base, next to the speaker and under the palm rest.
keyNumbers: About 3.8 V per cell
Roughly 11 to 12 Wh, a sixth of the pack
Only about 4 to 6 mm thick
details.madeOf: Thin layers of graphite and lithium metal oxide on copper and aluminium foils, separated by a porous plastic film and sealed in an aluminium-laminated pouch. A pouch is lighter and thinner than a hard can, so cells can be shaped to fill the case.

parts.name: Battery cell 1

parts.description: One of six flat lithium-ion pouch cells that together store about 70 watt-hours.

details.didYouKnow: Many battery cells are glued in with stretchy adhesive strips that let go when you pull them out slowly at a low angle, so the cell can be removed without prying.
details.howItWorks: Cells are wired in groups so their voltages add up: several in series give the roughly 11 to 13 V the laptop's power circuits expect, and pairs in parallel add capacity. A battery management chip watches every group's voltage and temperature and balances them so none is overcharged. This cell sits second from the left.
keyNumbers: Pack voltage roughly 11 to 13 V
Each cell charged to about 4.2 to 4.4 V when full
Held in place by stretch-release adhesive strips
details.madeOf: The same layered graphite and lithium metal oxide sandwich as its neighbours, in a laminated aluminium pouch. Identical cells are matched so they age evenly together.

parts.name: Battery cell 2

parts.description: One of six flat lithium-ion pouch cells that together store about 70 watt-hours.

details.didYouKnow: Many laptops learn your routine and pause charging at around 80 percent until shortly before you usually unplug, because sitting at 100 percent wears the cells faster.
details.howItWorks: This cell sits near the middle, just under the trackpad, so it supports the haptic engine and trackpad frame above it. Like the others, it gets warmer when charging fast or under heavy load, and the system slows charging if any cell runs too hot. Lithium cells are happiest at moderate temperatures and charge levels.
keyNumbers: Pack typically lasts about 1,000 full cycles before falling to roughly 80 percent capacity
Best kept between roughly 10 and 35 degrees C
Fast charge can reach about 50 percent in roughly 30 minutes
details.madeOf: Graphite anode and lithium metal oxide cathode layers in a liquid or gel electrolyte, inside a laminated aluminium pouch. The electrolyte lets ions move between the electrodes while the separator stops them touching.

parts.name: Battery cell 3

parts.description: One of six flat lithium-ion pouch cells that together store about 70 watt-hours.

details.didYouKnow: The roughly 100 Wh limit for carrying laptop batteries in airline cabins is why so few laptops have packs much bigger than that.
details.howItWorks: Sitting just right of centre under the trackpad, this cell works with cell 3 as part of the pack's middle section. The battery management system counts charge going in and out of the whole pack to estimate the percentage you see on screen. That estimate is recalibrated whenever the pack is nearly full or nearly empty.
keyNumbers: Pack of about 70 Wh in total
Gives roughly 15 to 20 hours of video playback
Weighs roughly 40 to 60 g
details.madeOf: Layered graphite, lithium metal oxide and a thin porous separator, sealed in a plastic-lined aluminium pouch. The plastic lining stops the electrolyte from reacting with the aluminium.

parts.name: Battery cell 4

parts.description: One of six flat lithium-ion pouch cells that together store about 70 watt-hours.

details.didYouKnow: A swollen laptop battery can lift the trackpad so it stops clicking properly, which is often the first sign people notice.
details.howItWorks: This cell sits second from the right, filling the space between the trackpad and the right palm rest. A pouch cell slowly swells as it ages, so the case leaves a little room around it. If a cell is damaged or badly aged, gas can build up and puff it out noticeably, which is a sign it needs replacing.
keyNumbers: Electrode layers each only tens of micrometres thick
Room left for swelling of roughly several percent of thickness
Holds about a sixth of the pack's 70 Wh
details.madeOf: Graphite and lithium metal oxide on thin metal foils, folded or stacked inside an aluminium-laminated pouch. Stacking many thin layers gives a big electrode area in a small space, which helps the cell deliver power quickly.

parts.name: Battery cell 5

parts.description: One of six flat lithium-ion pouch cells that together store about 70 watt-hours.

details.didYouKnow: Lithium-ion cells pack roughly two to three times more energy per kilogram than the nickel-metal hydride batteries that laptops used in the 1990s.
details.howItWorks: The outer right cell completes the pack, sitting at the right front next to the speaker. The cells' connections run to a small protection board that can cut the circuit if it sees a short, overcharging or overheating. When you plug in, the charging circuit on the logic board fills all six cells together.
keyNumbers: Pack of about 70 Wh across 6 cells
Battery makes up roughly a fifth of the laptop's weight
Charges at up to roughly 100 W with a fast charger
details.madeOf: The same graphite and lithium metal oxide pouch construction as the other five. Using several identical cells lets the pack be shaped around the trackpad while keeping production simple.

parts.name: Battery cell 6

parts.description: Pair of opposing woofers plus a tweeter in a sealed box; the opposed woofers cancel vibration.

details.didYouKnow: The sound leaves mostly through the grilles beside the keyboard, but some escapes through gaps around the keys too, which helps spread it out.
details.howItWorks: Two woofers face away from each other, so when one cone pushes forwards the other pushes backwards and their kicks on the case cancel out, stopping the whole laptop from buzzing at loud bass notes. A small tweeter adds clear high frequencies. The left speaker plays the left channel, and processing in the main chip shapes the sound so it seems wider than the laptop itself.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 drivers in each speaker box
Bass reaches down to roughly 80 to 100 Hz
Each box only about 1 cm tall
details.madeOf: Light diaphragm cones driven by copper voice coils and neodymium magnets, in a sealed plastic enclosure. The sealed box controls how the air inside springs back, which tightens the bass.

parts.name: Speaker (left)

parts.description: Pair of opposing woofers plus a tweeter in a sealed box; the opposed woofers cancel vibration.

details.didYouKnow: Opposed-woofer layouts like this come from high-end home subwoofers, where they are used for the same reason: to stop the box from shaking.
details.howItWorks: The right speaker plays the right channel, mirroring the left. Software tunes each speaker so that it never moves its cones further than they can safely go, letting such small drivers play surprisingly loud. Together the two boxes can create a spatial effect, using tricks that mimic how sound reaches your two ears.
keyNumbers: Six drivers in total across the two speakers
Covers up to roughly 20 kHz, the top of human hearing
Driver magnets weigh only a few grams
details.madeOf: Light cones, copper voice coils and small but powerful neodymium magnets in a sealed plastic box. Neodymium gives a strong magnetic push from very little weight.

parts.name: Speaker (right)

parts.description: Upper face of the aluminium unibody, cut out for the keyboard and trackpad.

details.didYouKnow: The tiny speaker grille holes are drilled or laser-cut after the case is machined, and there can be over a thousand of them on one laptop.
details.howItWorks: The top case is the face you rest your palms on, and the keyboard, trackpad and battery are all fixed to its underside. Because it is part of the same machined piece as the side walls, the whole base acts like a stiff tray that hardly flexes when you type or lift it by a corner. The speaker grilles are drilled straight through it either side of the keyboard.
keyNumbers: About 31 x 22 cm
Hundreds of tiny speaker holes drilled through it
Anodised layer typically about 10 to 25 micrometres thick
details.madeOf: Anodised aluminium alloy machined from a solid block. Anodising grows a hard oxide layer on the surface that resists scratches and takes the colour.

parts.name: Top case

parts.description: Side walls of the body, milled with the top case from one solid block of recycled aluminium.

details.didYouKnow: Machining laptop bodies from a single block went mainstream in 2008; recycling aluminium uses only about 5 percent of the energy needed to make it fresh from ore.
details.howItWorks: The side walls and top case start as one solid slab of aluminium, which computer-controlled cutters carve away until only a thin shell is left. With no joins or screwed-on panels, it is stiff and light, and the port openings and screw bosses are cut in the same process. Most of the starting block ends up as chips, which are collected and recycled.
keyNumbers: Whole laptop weighs roughly 1.5 to 1.6 kg
About 1.55 cm thick when closed
Most of the starting block is machined away
details.madeOf: Recycled aluminium alloy, typically a 6000-series alloy of aluminium with small amounts of magnesium and silicon. It machines cleanly, is strong for its weight and is endlessly recyclable.

parts.name: Unibody frame

parts.description: Removable aluminium base plate with rubber feet and intake vents for the fans.

details.didYouKnow: Using a laptop on a duvet or pillow can block the intakes underneath, which is why it can get hot and noisy in bed but stays quiet on a desk.
details.howItWorks: The bottom case closes the base and is held on by small screws, so it is the way in for repairs. Rubber feet lift the laptop slightly off the desk so air can reach the fan intakes in the base, and the case also helps spread a little heat. The underside usually carries the regulatory markings and serial number.
keyNumbers: Typically under 1 mm thick
Held by roughly 6 to 10 small screws
Feet lift the laptop about 1 to 2 mm
details.madeOf: A thin anodised aluminium plate with rubber or silicone feet. Aluminium is light, stiff enough for a large flat panel and conducts heat away from the components inside.

parts.name: Bottom case

parts.description: MagSafe charging port, two Thunderbolt/USB-C ports and the headphone jack, each on its own little board.

details.didYouKnow: The magnetic breakaway charging plug was reportedly inspired by the magnetic power cords used on some Japanese deep fryers and rice cookers, there to stop hot appliances being pulled off the counter.
details.howItWorks: The magnetic charging connector snaps on and pops off if someone trips over the cable, so the laptop is not dragged to the floor. The two USB-C ports carry Thunderbolt, which can run data, video and power through the same small plug, so you can charge through them too. Mounting each port on its own small board means a worn socket can be swapped without replacing the whole logic board.
keyNumbers: Thunderbolt data at up to roughly 40 to 120 Gbit per second
Magnetic charging up to roughly 100 to 140 W
USB-C plugs rated for roughly 10,000 insertions
details.madeOf: Stainless steel shells around the sockets, with gold-plated contacts on small circuit boards. Steel resists the wear of thousands of plug-ins, and gold resists corrosion so the contacts stay reliable.

parts.name: Left ports

parts.description: HDMI, a third Thunderbolt/USB-C port and an SD card slot.

details.didYouKnow: A USB-C plug is reversible because its pins are laid out symmetrically, and a chip in the cable or device works out which way up it went in.
details.howItWorks: The HDMI port plugs straight into TVs and projectors without an adapter, and the SD card slot reads camera memory cards directly. The third Thunderbolt port on this side means you can charge from either side of the desk. A controller on the logic board handles each type of connection and passes data to the main chip.
keyNumbers: HDMI can drive up to roughly 4K at 240 Hz or 8K at 60 Hz
SD card reading up to roughly 300 MB per second
USB-C connector has 24 pins
details.madeOf: Metal-shelled sockets with gold-plated contacts on small boards, set into openings machined through the aluminium side wall. The tight fit stops the sockets from wobbling when cables are pulled.

parts.name: Right ports

summary: A 14-inch aluminium laptop, modelled on laptops like the MacBook Pro: a single chip with the processor, graphics and memory, a mini-LED screen, a battery that fills the front of the base, and twin fans to keep it cool.
